To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the central DM density profiles of simulated galaxies are significantly flattened by outflows, and that (ii) the central DM profile slope depends on the stellar mass of a galaxy, and that (iii) the mass within 500 pc is constant over 4 orders of magnitude in stellar mass.

(1) The DM density profile of simulated galaxies is well fitted by a power law rhoDM propto 10^(0.5-0.35*log10(Mstar/1e8Msolar)*r^alpha where alpha is in the range -0.6 < alpha < -0.2, depending on Mstar.
the central dark matter and baryon distribution of galaxies is affected by outflows and that the central slope of DM profiles is shallower than predicted in DM-only simulations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the evolution of the central DM and baryon distribution in galaxies.
understanding the origin of the observed shallow inner DM profiles in galaxies.
the evolution of the central dark matter and baryonic profile of galaxies in a fully cosmological context and the effect of outflows on the central dark matter distribution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
outflows are a crucial element in the formation and evolution of galaxies, and that they play a major role in shaping the central DM distribution.

, in Lambda CDM cosmologies, the observed shallow central DM density profiles are not only consistent with the presence of baryons, but are a direct consequence of the interplay between gas, stars and DM.
the Lambda CDM model, as implemented in these simulations, does not predict cuspy DM density profiles in the inner regions of galaxies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
outflows are a key ingredient in the evolution of galaxies, and that they can explain the observed flattening of the central DM density profile.
, in the Lambda CDM paradigm, the inner DM distribution of galaxies is not cuspy.
the Lambda CDM paradigm, when combined with a physically motivated model for gas outflows, can successfully reproduce the observed central density distribution of DM in a variety of field galaxies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gas outflows, driven by SF and SNe, are a key physical mechanism that significantly alters the DM profile and the inner baryon content of galaxies.
the central DM density profile of a galaxy is not a `frozen' relic of its early formation but is strongly influenced by its subsequent evolution.
the central density profiles of DM and baryons in galaxies are intimately linked, and that the DM profile is significantly affected by the baryons in the galaxy, and not only by the DM potential.
